blocks.text: A skydiver leaves an aircraft and accelerates at nearly 9.81 m/s$^2$, but within about ten seconds the acceleration fades away and the fall settles at roughly 45 m/s. The same effect limits raindrops, ball-bearings in oil and cars on a motorway. The cause is fluid drag, a force that grows with speed until it balances the weight.

blocks.markdown: A body moving through a fluid experiences a **drag force** opposing its velocity. Two models cover most introductory problems. At low speeds, or in very viscous fluids (small bodies, oils), drag is approximately **linear**: $F_D=cv$, where $c$ (kg/s) is a drag constant. At the higher speeds typical of vehicles, sports balls and skydivers, the flow is turbulent and drag is **quadratic**: $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$. Here $\rho$ is the fluid density (kg/m$^3$), $C_d$ a dimensionless drag coefficient depending on shape, $A$ the frontal (projected) area (m$^2$) and $v$ the speed (m/s).

blocks.title: Quadratic drag force
blocks.text: $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$ directed opposite to the velocity. Typical values (representative only): $\rho_{air}\approx1.2$ kg/m$^3$ at sea level; $C_d\approx0.3$ for a streamlined car, about 1.0 for a skydiver in free fall and about 1.2 to 1.5 for an open parachute canopy.

blocks.caption: Doubling the speed multiplies the drag force by four and the power needed to overcome it by eight.

blocks.title: Estimating a drag force
blocks.prompt: A cyclist and bicycle present a frontal area $A=0.50$ m$^2$ with $C_d=0.90$ in air of density 1.2 kg/m$^3$. Find the drag force and the power needed to overcome it at 12 m/s.
blocks.answer: The drag force is about 39 N, requiring roughly 467 W to overcome it at 12 m/s.

blocks.markdown: **Terminal velocity (quadratic drag).** A body released from rest and falling vertically has weight $mg$ down and drag $F_D$ up. Newton's second law (down positive) gives $m\dot v=mg-\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$. As $v$ grows, drag grows, so the acceleration decreases. When the drag equals the weight, the acceleration is zero and the speed stops changing: this is the **terminal velocity** $v_t$.

blocks.latex: m\dot v=mg-\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2,\qquad \dot v=0\ \Rightarrow\ v_t=\sqrt{\frac{2mg}{\rho C_dA}}
blocks.caption: The terminal speed grows with $\sqrt{m}$ and falls with $\sqrt{\rho C_dA}$.

blocks.title: Skydiver terminal velocity
blocks.prompt: An 80 kg skydiver has $C_d=1.0$ and frontal area $0.70$ m$^2$ in air of density 1.2 kg/m$^3$. Find the terminal velocity ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Set acceleration to zero: weight equals drag.

blocks.answer: The terminal velocity is about 43.2 m/s.

blocks.markdown: **Linear drag in closed form.** For $F_D=cv$ the equation of motion is $m\dot v=mg-cv$, which is separable. Writing $v_t=mg/c$ for the terminal velocity and $\tau=m/c$ (s) for the **time constant**, integrating from $v=0$ at $t=0$ gives an exponential approach to $v_t$: after one time constant, the body has reached 63% of terminal speed.

blocks.caption: Exact solution of $m\dot v=mg-cv$ with $v(0)=0$; quadratic drag has a similar-looking but different solution $v=v_t\tanh(gt/v_t)$.

blocks.title: Sphere falling in oil
blocks.prompt: A small sphere of mass 0.020 kg falls from rest in oil with linear drag $F_D=cv$ and $c=0.50$ kg/s. Find the terminal velocity, the time constant and the velocity after 0.10 s ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$; neglect buoyancy).
blocks.answer: $v_t=0.392$ m/s, $\tau=0.040$ s and $v(0.10\ \text{s})=0.360$ m/s, about 92% of terminal speed.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Do not use $F_D=cv$ for a skydiver or $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$ for oil unless the regime fits. Terminal velocity is approached, never reached in finite time. Check the direction: drag always opposes the velocity, so it changes sign if the body moves upward. Keep units consistent: $A$ in m$^2$, $\rho$ in kg/m$^3$.

points: Quadratic drag $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$ is estimated from $C_d$, density, frontal area and speed; the power to overcome it grows as $v^3$.
Setting weight equal to drag gives the terminal velocity $v_t=\sqrt{2mg/(\rho C_dA)}$; for linear drag $v_t=mg/c$.

questions.stem: A car's aerodynamic drag follows $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$. If the speed is doubled, the drag force becomes

distractorRationale.a: Eight times is the factor for the power ($\propto v^3$), not the force.

questions.explanation: Quadratic drag is proportional to $v^2$, so doubling speed quadruples the force. The power needed to overcome it rises by a factor of eight.

questions.stem: A body falling vertically through air has reached terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The drag force is greater than the weight
The drag force equals the weight and the acceleration is zero

questions.correctOptionText: The drag force equals the weight and the acceleration is zero

distractorRationale.a: Drag grows to balance the weight, so it is not zero.
distractorRationale.b: The body falls at constant speed, not at rest.
distractorRationale.c: If drag exceeded weight the body would be decelerating.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: net force and acceleration are zero.

questions.explanation: At terminal velocity $mg-F_D=0$, so $\dot v=0$ and the speed is constant. The body keeps moving downward at $v_t$.

questions.stem: Two sky divers have identical shape and frontal area, but one has twice the mass of the other. Assuming quadratic drag, the heavier diver's terminal velocity is

distractorRationale.b: Would apply to linear drag, where $v_t\propto m$.
distractorRationale.c: Overestimates: it is a square-root dependence.

questions.explanation: From $v_t=\sqrt{2mg/(\rho C_dA)}$ with everything else equal, doubling $m$ multiplies $v_t$ by $\sqrt2$. A heavier body therefore falls faster in the end, but not in proportion to its weight.

questions.stem: For a sphere falling in a viscous oil with $F_D=cv$ and mass $m$, the time constant $\tau=m/c$ is the time it takes, starting from rest, for the speed to reach about

distractorRationale.a: Terminal velocity is approached only as $t\to\infty$.

questions.explanation: Setting $t=\tau$ in $v=v_t(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ gives $v=v_t(1-e^{-1})=0.632v_t$. The motion is effectively complete after a few time constants.

questions.stem: A skydiver has a terminal velocity of 50 m/s at sea level, where the air density is 1.2 kg/m$^3$. A second jump is made where the density is 0.4 kg/m$^3$ (one third of that value), with the same body position. The terminal velocity there is approximately

distractorRationale.d: Treats $v_t$ as inversely proportional to density.

questions.explanation: From $v_t=\sqrt{2mg/(\rho C_dA)}$, reducing $\rho$ by a factor of 3 increases $v_t$ by $\sqrt3=1.73$. Hence $v_t\approx50\times1.73=87$ m/s.

questions.stem: A car with $C_d=0.30$ and frontal area 2.2 m$^2$ travels at 30 m/s in air of density 1.2 kg/m$^3$. Find the aerodynamic drag force in newtons.
questions.explanation: $F_D=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2=\tfrac12(1.2)(0.30)(2.2)(900)=356.4$ N. The corresponding power at that speed is about 10.7 kW.

questions.stem: A parachutist and equipment of total mass 90 kg descend under a canopy of frontal area 40 m$^2$ with $C_d=1.5$ in air of density 1.2 kg/m$^3$. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the terminal velocity in m/s.
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity $mg=\tfrac12\rho C_dAv_t^2$, so $v_t=\sqrt{2(90)(9.81)/(1.2\times1.5\times40)}=\sqrt{24.53}=4.95$ m/s. This is slow enough for a safe landing, which is why large canopies are used.

questions.stem: A small bead of mass 0.050 kg falls from rest in a viscous liquid with linear drag $F_D=cv$ and $c=2.0$ kg/s. Neglecting buoyancy and taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its speed at $t=0.050$ s in m/s.
questions.explanation: The terminal velocity is $mg/c=0.05(9.81)/2.0=0.2453$ m/s and the time constant is $m/c=0.025$ s. At $t=0.050$ s, $t/\tau=2$, so $v=0.2453(1-e^{-2})=0.2453(0.8647)=0.2121$ m/s.

questions.stem: Derive the terminal velocity of a body falling vertically through air with quadratic drag, and explain physically why the acceleration decreases to zero rather than the body continuing to speed up.
markingGuide: Draw the FBD: weight $mg$ down, drag $\tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2$ up.
Drag increases with $v^2$, so the net downward force decreases as speed rises.
At $v_t$ the net force is zero so the speed is constant; $v_t$ is approached asymptotically.
questions.explanation: Weight is constant but drag rises with speed, so the net force shrinks to zero. The balance point defines the terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A particle falls from rest in a fluid with linear drag. Derive the closed-form velocity $v(t)$ by separating variables, identify the terminal velocity and the time constant, and compare the initial acceleration with the free-fall value.
markingGuide: At $t=0$, $v=0$ so drag is zero and the initial acceleration is $g$; it decays exponentially.
questions.explanation: Linear drag makes the equation of motion a first-order linear ODE, which separates cleanly. The exponential form shows the approach to $v_t$ and the time scale $m/c$.
